title: Physics I
description: Physics I introduces mechanics as the disciplined modeling of motion, forces, energy, momentum, rotation, gravitation, oscillations, waves, fluids, and measurement. The course emphasizes conceptual understanding, calculus-based problem solving, laboratory reasoning, uncertainty analysis, computational modeling, and transfer to engineering, life science, and physical science contexts.

topics.title: Physical Modeling, Measurement, Units, and Uncertainty
topics.description: Students begin by learning how physics turns messy reality into measured quantities, models, estimates, and testable claims.

children.title: Models and approximations
children.description: The point is to learn that physics is built from idealized models chosen for a purpose.

children.title: Units and dimensional reasoning
children.description: Students use units as a guardrail for equations and a tool for discovering scaling laws.

children.title: Measurement and uncertainty
children.description: Real data have uncertainty, so students must report results with defensible precision.

topics.title: Vectors, Coordinate Systems, and Mathematical Tools for Mechanics
topics.description: This topic builds the mathematical language needed to describe motion, force, and change in one, two, and three dimensions.

children.title: Vector representation
children.description: Mechanics becomes clearer when displacement, velocity, force, and momentum are treated as vectors.

children.title: Products and projections
children.description: Dot and cross products encode work, torque, angular momentum, and geometry.

children.title: Calculus for motion
children.description: Derivatives and integrals connect position, velocity, acceleration, work, and accumulated change.

topics.title: Kinematics in One and Two Dimensions
topics.description: Students learn to describe motion before explaining its causes, using position, velocity, acceleration, and graphical reasoning.

children.title: One-dimensional motion
children.description: Students learn to connect equations, graphs, and physical motion along a line.

children.title: Two-dimensional motion
children.description: Independent component analysis makes curved motion manageable.

children.title: Nonuniform motion
children.description: Real motion often changes with time, so students practice calculus-based descriptions.

topics.title: Newton's Laws, Free-Body Diagrams, and Force Models
topics.description: This module connects motion to interactions through disciplined free-body diagrams and Newtonian dynamics.

children.title: Newton's laws
children.description: Newton's laws define how interactions change motion and how objects push on each other.

children.title: Free-body diagrams
children.description: A clear diagram is the main technology for solving force problems correctly.

children.title: Common force models
children.description: Students learn the standard force laws used across mechanics problems.

topics.title: Applications of Newtonian Dynamics
topics.description: Students apply force laws to realistic systems including friction, drag, circular motion, constraints, and coupled bodies.

children.title: Constrained systems
children.description: Pulleys, inclines, and connected bodies teach students to translate geometry into equations.

children.title: Circular motion
children.description: Curved motion requires centripetal acceleration even when speed is constant.

children.title: Non-ideal forces
children.description: Drag and resistance introduce realistic motion and simple differential equations.

topics.title: Work, Energy, Power, and Conservative Forces
topics.description: This topic introduces energy as a powerful alternative to force-by-force analysis.

children.title: Work and kinetic energy
children.description: Work-energy methods often solve motion problems more simply than forces alone.

children.title: Work by constant and variable forces
Potential energy
children.description: Conservative forces allow motion to be analyzed through stored energy landscapes.

children.title: Energy diagrams and dissipation
children.description: Students learn to reason qualitatively and quantitatively about allowed motion and losses.

topics.title: Momentum, Impulse, Collisions, and Systems of Particles
topics.description: Students learn conservation of momentum and center-of-mass methods for interactions and multi-body systems.

children.title: Momentum and impulse
children.description: Momentum tracks motion through interactions over time, especially when forces are large and brief.

children.title: Collisions
children.description: Collision analysis combines momentum conservation with energy bookkeeping.

children.title: Center of mass
children.description: Multi-particle systems can often be simplified by tracking the motion of their center of mass.

topics.title: Rotational Kinematics, Torque, and Rigid-Body Dynamics
topics.description: This module extends mechanics from particles to rotating bodies and distributed mass.

children.title: Rotational variables
children.description: Angular position, velocity, and acceleration mirror linear kinematics but require careful units and geometry.

children.title: Torque and rotational inertia
children.description: Rotation depends on where forces act and how mass is distributed.

children.title: Rotational energy and dynamics
children.description: Students connect torque, angular acceleration, and rotational kinetic energy.

children.title: Rotational form of Newton's second law

topics.title: Angular Momentum, Rolling Motion, and Gyroscopic Effects
topics.description: Students learn why angular momentum is conserved, how rolling links translation and rotation, and why rotating systems behave unexpectedly.

children.title: Angular momentum conservation
children.description: Angular momentum explains rotation in isolated systems from skaters to planets.

children.title: Rolling motion
children.description: Rolling combines translation and rotation through a no-slip constraint.

children.title: Gyroscopes and precession
children.description: Rotating objects respond to torque in ways that reveal vector angular momentum.

topics.title: Static Equilibrium, Elasticity, and Introductory Engineering Mechanics
topics.description: This topic develops balance laws for structures, beams, materials, and biological or engineered load-bearing systems.

children.title: Equilibrium conditions
children.description: Statics applies force and torque balance to objects that are not accelerating.

children.title: Structures and load paths
children.description: Students learn how forces flow through real supports, beams, and frames.

children.title: Elasticity
children.description: Materials deform under load, making mechanics relevant to engineering, biology, and design.

topics.title: Gravitation, Orbits, and Central-Force Motion
topics.description: Students connect Newton's universal law to planetary motion, satellites, escape speed, and inverse-square forces.

children.title: Newtonian gravitation
children.description: Universal gravitation connects falling objects, planetary motion, and satellite systems.

children.title: Orbital motion
children.description: Students see circular and elliptical orbits as consequences of central forces.

children.title: Energy and angular momentum in gravity
children.description: Conservation laws give a deep view of bounded and unbounded motion.

topics.title: Oscillations, Resonance, and Introductory Waves
topics.description: This module develops periodic motion and wave behavior as a bridge from mechanics to sound, fields, and modern physics.

children.title: Simple harmonic motion
children.description: Small oscillations appear throughout physics because many stable systems are approximately quadratic near equilibrium.

children.title: Damping and driving
children.description: Real oscillators lose energy and can resonate when driven at the right frequency.

children.title: Waves and sound
children.description: Waves extend oscillation ideas through space and prepare students for later E&M and optics.

topics.title: Fluids, Pressure, Buoyancy, and Flow
topics.description: Students study continuum behavior in liquids and gases, including hydrostatics and ideal-flow principles.

children.title: Pressure and hydrostatics
children.description: Fluids at rest transmit force through pressure that varies with depth.

children.title: Buoyancy
children.description: Archimedes' principle explains floating, sinking, and apparent weight.

children.title: Flow models
children.description: Introductory flow ideas connect conservation principles to fluids in motion.

topics.title: Thermal Physics and Energy Transfer Preview
topics.description: This topic introduces temperature, kinetic theory, heat, and the thermodynamic ideas often paired with Physics I.

children.title: Temperature and kinetic theory
children.description: Thermal physics links microscopic motion to macroscopic temperature and pressure.

children.title: Heat and work
children.description: Students distinguish energy transfer by thermal interaction from mechanical work.

children.title: Transport and applications
children.description: Thermal processes show how energy moves through matter and systems.

topics.title: Laboratory Modeling, Computation, and Mechanics Project
topics.description: The course culminates in careful experimentation, uncertainty analysis, computational modeling, and a polished mechanics investigation.

children.title: Experimental design
children.description: Students learn to ask a measurable question and design a test that can actually answer it.

children.title: Computational mechanics
children.description: Numerical models let students study motion when analytic solutions are hard or impossible.

children.title: Scientific communication
children.description: A Physics I project requires clear reasoning, honest uncertainty, and polished presentation.
